newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Despair hangs over chic Australian ski town.
newsitem.headline: Despair hangs over chic Australian ski town.

text.p: Australia's Thredbo ski resort, normally the place to be seen in winter for the chic and the fashionable, was plunged into despair on Thursday as hope faded for up to 20 people trapped by a midnight landslide.

People in the affluent, tight-knit community nestled high in the Snowy Mountains showed little interest in the usual partying and skiing as rescuers worked through the night in freezing temperatures in search of some of their friends and co-workers.

Police said up to 20 people were inside the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges when the landslide occurred just before midnight on Wednesday at the Thredbo Alpine Village in the Snowy Mountains, 400km (250 miles) south of Sydney.
As a human chain of rescuers worked painstakingly under arc lights, police said that one body had been found.

A police spokeswoman told Reuters they had confirmed 18 people -- 11 men and seven women -- were in the Bimbadeen lodge, including a middle-aged couple from the United States and a woman from New Zealand.
"There were two people from California, a 46-year-old-man and his 41-year-old wife," the spokeswoman said.
The age of the New Zealand woman was not known. The remaining 15 people in the Bimbadeen lodge were all from New South Wales state, the spokeswoman said.
One heart-rending story on a day of tragedy emerged when police said a woman, walking with her husband on a road near the lodges, was swept away by the landslide.

"He was walking on the road with his wife, he happened to be a few paces ahead of her," regional police commander Bruce Johnston told reporters. "She was gathered up in the slippage. We haven't found her yet."
Eyewitnesses reported hearing voices from the rubble shortly after the landslide but police searching with fibre optic cameras said there had been no sign of life in almost 20 hours.
"Those cries stopped fairly early in the piece," Johnston said, adding that more landslides were virtually inevitable.

Numbed and subdued, tourists and resort workers sat quietly in coffee shops, or gathered on a small ridge 100 metres across from the swathe of mud and rubble which marks where the two lodges once stood.
"It looks like someone has taken a great big bulldozer and just drove over both the lodges and they just slid down the hill," one unidentified witness told reporters.
The nearby ski slopes were almost empty despite perfect skiing weather. Some shops closed their doors for the day.
"It's pretty close here...you have lots of friends, you work together and play together, ski, and it's really sad," local chef Patrick Scott told Reuters.
Sydney businessman Bill Reeve, 58, told Reuters he doubted any survivors would be found in the rubble.
"The mud was soggy and soft, it seemed, around me. It would have filled every void," said Reeve, adding he was staying near Bimbadeen lodge when he heard a "roar and then a crack".

Australia is to host an alpine skiing world cup aerial event in neighbouring Victoria state from Friday and Kirstie Marshall, Australia's defending world champion, said the event would be overshadowed by the catastrophe in Thredbo.
"The skiing community is very small and everyone has been affected by this," Marshall told reporters.
Around Thredbo, some people were readying to leave their devastated playground.
"It's a bit hard to go on skiiing knowing this has happened," Lakshman Jayaran, 28, told Reuters.
